analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from permanently replacing workers who go on strike or exercise union rights.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 16 Senate Democrats, was referred to the Senate labor committee in October 2000 and died there without ever reaching a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, an employer can hire "permanent replacements" for workers who go on strike, meaning those workers can lose their jobs for exercising the right to strike. This bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act to make that illegal: employers could no longer grant anyone permanent replacement status during a labor dispute, or give hiring preferences to people who worked during the dispute over strikers who came back or offered to come back. The bill was introduced in late October 2000, with less than three months left in the Congress, and was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who join a union or participate in a strike keep the right to reclaim their jobs when the dispute ends, rather than being displaced forever by replacement hires. This protects the economic power behind collective bargaining for unionized employees, including railroad workers covered by the Railway Labor Act.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers from offering or granting anyone "permanent replacement employee" status for bargaining-unit work performed during a labor dispute, so a striker cannot be permanently displaced for striking.

Prohibits employers from giving any employment preference to someone because they worked during the dispute, or said they were willing to, over a striker who is working or has unconditionally offered to return to work.
Applies the same protections to railroad and airline workers by amending the Railway Labor Act, not just private-sector workers under the National Labor Relations Act.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with unionized workforces would lose their ability to permanently replace striking workers, which has been a legal tool for keeping strikes bounded and for continuing operations during a dispute. Strikes could become longer and more costly for employers, and the costs could reach consumers and shareholders of affected companies.

drawbacks.text: Employers and business groups have long argued that the ability to hire permanent replacements is a lawful counterweight to the right to strike; removing it could make strikes longer, more disruptive to customers and supply chains, and riskier for employers to manage.

The bill protects strikers' jobs but does not address the underlying contract disputes, so a strike could still drag on with neither side under added pressure to settle; critics would say this shifts leverage toward unions without shortening conflicts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a real, concrete protection to striking workers — keeping their jobs — at a real cost to employers, who would lose a long-standing legal tool for operating during strikes and pressing for settlement. For working people in unionized workplaces, the benefit is direct and substantial; the costs fall mostly on employers and, indirectly, on consumers if strikes grow longer. The bill died too early in the process for any of these tradeoffs to be tested in debate or amendment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with under three months left in the Congress and referred to the Senate labor committee, which never acted on it, so it never reached the Senate floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced S. 3249 on October 26, 2000, joined by 15 Democratic colleagues including Wellstone, Kennedy, Boxer, and Kerry; all 16 sponsors were Democrats.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action appears in the record: the committee held no markup and the bill never received a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and business interests are better off because the bill died: they retain the legal ability to hire permanent replacements for striking workers and to prefer strikebreakers in future hiring. The bill's sponsors gained nothing from the outcome.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on October 26, 2000.

for.name: 15 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Wellstone, Kennedy, Murray, Feingold, Bingaman, Boxer, Mikulski, Sarbanes, Dodd, Kerry, Akaka, Lieberman, Leahy, Baucus, and Rockefeller

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 26, 2000 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with only weeks left in the Congress the bill never progressed to a vote where party splits would have been recorded.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to grant permanent replacement status during labor disputes, removing a legal tool for continuing operations during strikes and pressuring settlements. Their interest in keeping that tool runs against strikers' interest in keeping their jobs.
Business supplying replacement workers during strikes would lose the market for permanent replacement placements, since no one could be granted permanent status for dispute-period work.
Covered directly by the Railway Labor Act amendment, carriers would lose permanent-replacement rights in craft disputes, but they also gain clearer rules for reinstating workers who offer to return.
